introduction-the-failure-of-the-monolith.core: A single central data team that must understand and clean every domain's data becomes a bottleneck with poor quality. Data mesh inverts this: domains own their analytical data, and governance is shared and automated.

first_principles.problem: Every team dumps raw data into a central lake, and a central data team tries to make sense of it all, without building any of it. They interrupt domain teams to decode fields, can't fix problems at the source, and accumulate a queue of requests that takes weeks to clear.
truths: The people who build a system understand its data best.
One team's capacity can't grow with the number of domains.
Teams that create data rarely benefit from making it usable unless it's their job.
derivation: Recognise the failure modes: **bottleneck, domain ignorance, low quality, slow iteration, misaligned incentives**.
**Decentralise ownership**: give analytical data to the domains that produce it.
**Federate governance** so decentralisation doesn't become chaos.
Follow the **microservices** analogy: owners, interfaces, and a shared platform.

analogy.title: One librarian for a whole city
analogy.story: Every book in the city must go through one librarian who catalogues, translates and summarises it, even books in languages they don't speak. As the city grows, readers wait weeks and summaries get worse.
analogy.breaks: Authors summarising their own books could create a mess of formats. Data mesh needs shared standards (governance) to stay joinable.

example.title: "What does shipping_code_99 mean?"
example.scenario: A central data engineer is blocked on a field the shipping team invented.

steps.label: Monolith
steps.detail: Knowledge lives in the source team, but the work lives in the central team.

steps.label: Mesh
steps.detail: The shipping team publishes a documented dataset where code 99 is already explained.

example.outcome: you see the core problem: ownership and knowledge are in different places.

points: Central teams don't scale with domains.

check.q: Why can't the central team just fix data quality problems?
check.a: They don't own the source systems, so they can only patch symptoms downstream, not fix causes.

principle-1-domain-oriented-ownership.core: The team that produces data is responsible for publishing a clean, documented, analytical view of it, just as it owns its service's code and on-call. Domain boundaries follow DDD bounded contexts.

first_principles.problem: Checkout emits raw logs to Kafka and considers its job done. Months later a central team produces a checkout table with gaps and misinterpretations, because only the checkout team knows that code 7 is Apple Pay or that PENDING orders older than 24 h are actually failures.
truths: Producers hold the context needed to interpret data.
Ownership drives quality when problems come back to the owner.
Operational APIs aren't designed for analytics.
derivation: Assign each **domain** (Checkout, Inventory, Shipping, Identity) ownership of its analytical data.
Draw boundaries from **bounded contexts** (DDD).
Publish **curated, documented, SLA-backed datasets**, not raw tables.
Treat schema changes like API changes: **communicated and versioned**.
Give domains **embedded data skills** by hiring or upskilling.

analogy.title: Each restaurant writes its own menu
analogy.story: In a food court, each restaurant describes its own dishes (ingredients, allergens, spice level) rather than a central manager guessing. The restaurant knows its food, and it's accountable when the description is wrong.
analogy.breaks: Menus rarely change shape. Datasets do, so domains must version and announce schema changes like public APIs.

branches.label: Principle
children: You build it, you own the data

example.title: Checkout publishes its own orders dataset
example.scenario: Instead of raw logs, Checkout publishes `orders_daily` with business rules applied.

steps.label: Encode knowledge
steps.detail: Map payment code 7 to 'apple_pay', and mark PENDING older than 24 h as 'failed'.

steps.label: Publish
steps.detail: A documented dataset with a freshness SLA.

steps.label: Own
steps.detail: Quality issues go to Checkout's backlog, not a central queue.

example.outcome: consumers get correct data from the people who understand it, without waiting weeks.

check.q: How is this different from each team owning its own database?
check.a: Domains also publish an analytical interface (curated, queryable datasets), not just private operational databases behind APIs.

principle-2-data-as-a-product.core: Treat a dataset like a product: code, data, metadata, access control and quality checks packaged together, discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, self-describing, interoperable, secure, natively accessible and valuable on its own. Version breaking changes.

first_principles.problem: In the central model, data is exhaust: a by-product dumped somewhere and forgotten. Consumers can't find it, don't know what fields mean, can't trust its freshness, and get broken when someone renames a column.
truths: People only depend on things they can find and trust.
Changing an interface breaks its consumers.
Quality guarantees mean nothing without checks.
derivation: Package **code, data, metadata, access control, quality checks** together.
Meet the **eight qualities**: discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, self-describing, interoperable, secure, natively accessible, valuable on its own.
Publish **SLOs** (e.g. updated by 03:00 UTC) and test them automatically.
Use a **schema registry** and **versioning**: breaking change means a new version with a deprecation timeline, additive changes otherwise.

analogy.title: A well-maintained software package
analogy.story: A good npm package has a name you can find, a stable install path, a README, a version number, tests, and a maintainer. You'd never depend on a random script someone emailed you, and data should be held to the same standard.
analogy.breaks: A package's code doesn't change after release. A data product's contents change daily, so freshness and quality must be monitored continuously, not just at publish time.

example.title: Renaming a column without breaking finance

steps.label: Breaking
steps.detail: Renaming is breaking, so it becomes a new version, not an in-place change.

steps.label: Overlap
steps.detail: v1 and v2 run side by side while consumers migrate.

steps.label: Retire
steps.detail: v1 is removed after the timeline, with the catalog showing who still reads it.

code.text:
s3://data-mesh/checkout/orders-daily/v1/   (deprecated, retire 2027-01-15)
s3://data-mesh/checkout/orders-daily/v2/   (current: amount_cents, Avro schema id 42)

example.outcome: producers can evolve, and consumers never wake up to broken dashboards.

points: A data product = code + data + metadata + access + checks.

check.q: How do you handle schema evolution in a mesh?
check.a: A schema registry, backward-compatible additive changes where possible, and new versions with a deprecation timeline for breaking ones, enforced by the platform.

principle-3-self-serve-data-platform.core: Domain ownership only works if publishing a data product is easy. A platform team provides self-serve storage, pipelines, schema registry, access control, catalog and monitoring, ideally driven by one declarative config file.

first_principles.problem: Telling every product team "you now own pipelines, storage, IAM, schema registries and monitoring" is an unfunded mandate. They're building features and won't become Spark and bucket-policy experts.
truths: Most infrastructure needs are the same across domains.
Repeated boilerplate is slow and error-prone.
Teams adopt what's easy and avoid what's hard.
derivation: Create a **platform team** that builds an internal developer platform for data.
Offer **storage provisioning, pipeline scaffolding, schema registry, access control, catalog registration, SLO monitoring, serverless compute**.
Aim for **one config file** per data product: name, owner, output, schedule, SLA, schema, readers, PII columns, checks.
The platform **provisions and enforces** everything from that file, with no Terraform or IAM from the domain.

analogy.title: A shopping-mall operator
analogy.story: Each shop runs its own business, but the mall provides electricity, security, card terminals, cleaning and signage. A new shop fills in one lease form and plugs in, without building its own power plant.
analogy.breaks: A mall is built once. A data platform must keep evolving with new storage, compute and policy needs, so it's a long-term product, not a project.

example.title: Publishing a product from one file
example.scenario: The Inventory team wants a daily `stock_levels` product.

steps.label: Declare
steps.detail: Name, owner, output path, schedule, SLA, schema, readers, PII columns, checks.

steps.label: Provision
steps.detail: The platform creates buckets or tables, a dbt or Airflow job, IAM and catalog entries.

steps.label: Operate
steps.detail: Freshness and quality checks run automatically, and failures notify Inventory.

code.text:
name: stock_levels
domain: inventory
owner: inventory-team@company.com
output: {format: parquet, path: inventory/stock-levels/v1/}
schedule: "0 2 * * *"
sla: {freshness_hours: 24}
readers: [analytics, supply-chain]
pii_columns: []
checks: [not_null: sku, row_count_min: 10000]

example.outcome: a domain team ships a governed data product in a day without becoming infrastructure experts.

check.q: What happens to data mesh without a self-serve platform?
check.a: Domain ownership becomes an unfunded mandate: teams either refuse, or build inconsistent, fragile infrastructure.

principle-4-federated-computational-gove.core: Governance is agreed by a federation of domain representatives and enforced automatically by the platform at publish time. Standardise only what interoperability needs (keys, time formats, PII, schema registration) and leave the rest to domains.

first_principles.problem: Without shared rules, Sales uses an integer user_id, Support keys by email and Shipping uses a legacy customer_code, so joins become archaeology. But a central committee reviewing every change recreates the bottleneck mesh was meant to remove.
truths: Data can only be joined if identifiers and formats agree.
derivation: **Federated**: a council of domain representatives agrees policies.
**Computational**: encode policies as code and **reject non-compliant products at publish**, like CI.
**Global** (mandatory): `customer_uuid` format, ISO 8601 UTC timestamps, PII handling, retention, schema registration.
**Local** (domain choice): internal names, transformation logic, tools, refresh beyond the minimum.
Examples: schema validation, automated PII detection, SLO breach marking, access-policy templates.

analogy.title: Building codes for a city
analogy.story: Neighbourhoods design their own buildings, but every building must meet the city's code: fire exits, electrical standards, accessibility. Inspectors don't review aesthetics. And in this city, the code is checked automatically when plans are submitted, not by a monthly inspection that never happens.
analogy.breaks: Building codes rarely change. Data standards evolve, so the federation must be able to version policies and roll them out without breaking existing products.

example.title: A product rejected at publish
example.scenario: Support tries to publish `tickets` keyed by integer `cust_id` with an unmasked email column.

steps.label: Interop
steps.detail: The platform requires the global `customer_uuid` for customer joins.

steps.label: Privacy
steps.detail: The scanner detects emails, so the column must be declared PII and masked.

steps.label: Autonomy
steps.detail: Everything else (column names, dbt vs Spark) is Support's choice.

code.text:
publish tickets@v1 … FAILED
  ✗ join key 'cust_id' (int) — must use customer_uuid (UUID v4)
  ✗ column 'email' looks like PII — declare in pii_columns and mask

example.outcome: datasets stay joinable and compliant without a human approval queue.

points: Policies that aren't automated don't exist in practice.

check.a: Only rules enforced automatically by the platform scale and actually get followed. Documents and audits don't.

data-mesh-vs-data-lake-vs-data-warehouse.core: Warehouses suit well-defined reporting with a small central team, lakes suit exploratory analytics and ML on raw data, and mesh suits large organisations with many autonomous domains. Each fails differently, so choose by organisational scale and maturity.

first_principles.problem: Data mesh is fashionable, but it costs quarters of platform work and a culture shift. Adopting it too early slows a small company down. Adopting too late leaves a large one stuck behind a central bottleneck.
truths: Every architecture has a characteristic failure mode.
Organisational structure shapes which architecture works.
Platform investment must come before domain ownership.
derivation: **Warehouse**: central team, schema-on-write, fast to value (weeks). Fails as a bottleneck at scale.
**Lake**: central team, schema-on-read, flexible. Fails as a "data swamp".
**Mesh**: domain ownership, federated standards, slow to value (quarters). Fails as silos if governance is weak.
Choose mesh only with roughly **5–10+ growing domains**, a visibly **bottlenecked central team**, **mature domain teams** and **leadership willing to fund the platform**.

analogy.title: Kitchen setups by restaurant size
analogy.story: A café needs one cook and one menu (warehouse). A test kitchen keeps every raw ingredient for experiments (lake). A huge food hall needs independent stalls with shared hygiene rules and utilities (mesh). Opening a food hall to sell coffee is overkill.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants can switch formats by renting new space. Moving from warehouse to mesh is an organisational change over many quarters.

example.title: Two companies, two answers
example.scenario: A 20-engineer startup vs. a 2,000-engineer marketplace with 30 domains.

steps.label: Startup
steps.detail: One warehouse with dbt and a small analytics team gets value in weeks.

steps.label: Marketplace
steps.detail: The central team has a 6-week backlog and domains have data skills, so invest in the platform, then onboard domains one at a time.

example.outcome: architecture choice follows organisational reality rather than trends.

points: Each architecture has its own failure mode.
Mesh needs scale, maturity and a platform.

check.q: What's the main failure mode of a poorly governed mesh?
check.a: Silos: domains publish incompatible data that can't be joined or trusted across the organisation.
